--- title: "Spatial and temporal cross-validation" description: "A score says how well a model predicts stations as far from its fitted data as the held-out ones were. Blocks as wide as the patches in a model's errors test new areas, and a forecast is tested only on years after those it was fitted to." order: 2 categories: [validation, spatial-temporal] --- ## Folds decide how far each prediction has to reach [Spatial and temporal dependence](../06-assumptions-limitations/spatial-and-temporal-dependence.qmd) found that a model's errors gather in patches on the map, and that spatial blocks score a model lower than cross-validation by site does. It left two choices open: how large the blocks should be, and how to hold out time for a model that forecasts. This page makes both. A cross-validated score says how well a model predicts stations as far from its fitted data as the held-out ones were, so choosing the folds means choosing that distance to match the model's use. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The score falls with distance to the fitted data For every held-out station, the **distance to the nearest fitted station** is how far away the closest station the model was fitted to lies. Folds of single stations often leave the station's own site in the fitted data, so that distance is short. Folds of sites push it out to the next site, and blocks push it across the block. The further away the fitted data, the less a model can lean on what its neighbours caught, and the larger its error. No distance is right in general. A model that fills the gaps between monitored sites is used close to its data, and folds of sites match that use. A habitat map of an area nobody has surveyed is used far from its data, and blocks match it. Choose the folds whose distance matches the use, and report the distance with the score. Each scheme on this page holds out every station once, so its pooled score, from [Cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd), can be compared with the others'. ## Blocks as wide as the error patches test new areas A held-out site is predicted too well when a fitted site in the same patch shares what the inputs miss. Blocks take that help away only if each block is at least as wide as a patch, so that most of a held-out site's patch is held out with it. The width of the patches comes from the errors of a model fitted without position. Take every pair of sites, group the pairs by the distance between them, and for each distance work out the correlation between the two sites' errors. This is a **correlogram**. Pairs in the same patch have errors that lean the same way, so at short distances the correlation is above zero. It falls to zero where the patches end, at the patches' **range**. Blocks should be at least that wide. Wider blocks change the question little but cost something: there are fewer of them, so the blocks that happen to share a fold sway the score more. Set the size from the errors before looking at the score. A size chosen for the score it gives makes the score a choice as well. ## An expanding window fits each round only to earlier years Holding out one year at a time fits each model to all the other years, later ones included. A forecast never has the later years. An **expanding window** fits the model to the first years, tests it on the next, and adds a year each round, so every tested year comes after the years its model was fitted to. ::: {.diagram} ![An expanding window over six years. Each round is fitted only to the years before the year it tests, and the window grows by a year each round. Leaving one year out, for contrast, fits to later years as well, which a forecast would not have.](img/expanding-window.svg){fig-alt="Two ways of holding out years, over six years of a survey. Expanding window, in four rounds: round 1 is fitted to years 1 and 2 and tests year 3; round 2 is fitted to years 1 to 3 and tests year 4; round 3 is fitted to years 1 to 4 and tests year 5; round 4 is fitted to years 1 to 5 and tests year 6. Later years are never used, and the tested years are pooled into one score. Below, for contrast, leave one year out: year 3 is tested by a model fitted to years 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6, so years 4 to 6, which a forecast would not have, help to predict it."} ::: The first rounds fit to few years, so the window starts once there is enough data to fit a model. Each round's tested year is a forecast one year ahead; pooled, they score the model as it would be used. ## Worked example The model is the random forest of [Forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd). As on [Cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd), it uses all the survey's sites, and every scheme has five folds. Each forest has 100 trees, so that the many refits stay quick. ### Preparing the data Each site's position is the centre of its stations. Distances are worked out in kilometres from longitude and latitude, using the length of a degree at the survey's latitude, 42° N. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |> # the centre of each site's stations mutate(site_lon = mean(longitude), site_lat = mean(latitude), .by = site_id) environment <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season") all_eight <- c(environment, "longitude", "latitude") forest_on <- function(vars) { recipe(reformulate(vars, "abundance"), data = survey) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> workflow(rand_forest(trees = 100) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |> set_mode("regression")) } # every station's out-of-fold prediction, in the survey's order out_of_fold <- function(vars, folds) { fit_resamples(forest_on(vars), folds, control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |> collect_predictions() |> arrange(.row) } km_between <- function(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2) { sqrt(((lat1 - lat2) * 111)^2 + ((lon1 - lon2) * 111 * cos(42 * pi / 180))^2) } # for each held-out station, the distance to the nearest fitted station nearest_km <- function(split) { fitted <- analysis(split) held <- assessment(split) map2_dbl(held$longitude, held$latitude, \(lon, lat) min(km_between(lon, lat, fitted$longitude, fitted$latitude))) } tibble(stations = nrow(survey), sites = n_distinct(survey$site_id), years = n_distinct(survey$survey_year)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| sites| years| |--------:|-----:|-----:| | 800| 160| 6|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, KFold, cross_val_predict from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() # the centre of each site's stations centre = survey.groupby("site_id")[["longitude", "latitude"]].transform("mean") survey["site_lon"] = centre["longitude"] survey["site_lat"] = centre["latitude"] observed = survey["abundance"].to_numpy() environment = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season"] all_eight = environment + ["longitude", "latitude"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] def forest_on(columns): numeric = [c for c in columns if c not in categorical] recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical), ]) return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), # max_features="sqrt" draws a few inputs at each question, as ranger does. ("model", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=1))]) # every station's out-of-fold prediction, in the survey's order def out_of_fold(columns, folds): return cross_val_predict(forest_on(columns), survey[columns], observed, cv=folds) def km_between(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2): return np.sqrt(((lat1 - lat2) * 111) ** 2 + ((lon1 - lon2) * 111 * np.cos(np.radians(42))) ** 2) lon = survey["longitude"].to_numpy() lat = survey["latitude"].to_numpy() # for each held-out station, the distance to the nearest fitted station def nearest_km(fit_rows, held_rows): return km_between(lon[held_rows, None], lat[held_rows, None], lon[None, fit_rows], lat[None, fit_rows]).min(axis=1) pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)], "sites": [survey["site_id"].nunique()], "years": [survey["survey_year"].nunique()]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | sites | years | |-----------:|--------:|--------:| | 800 | 160 | 6 | ::: ::: ::: ### Nearby sites' errors lean the same way A forest on the six environmental inputs, without position, is cross-validated by site. Each site's error is its catch over all visits divided by the catch the forest predicted, on a log scale so that twice and half as many count as equal and opposite. The correlogram then compares the errors of every pair of sites up to 120 km apart. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1) by_site <- group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = 5) site_errors <- survey |> mutate(predicted = out_of_fold(environment, by_site)$.pred) |> summarise(lon = first(site_lon), lat = first(site_lat), # +1 so that a site with no catch has an error too error = log((sum(abundance) + 1) / (sum(predicted) + 1)), .by = site_id) site_pairs <- cross_join(site_errors, site_errors, suffix = c("_a", "_b")) |> filter(site_id_a != site_id_b) |> mutate(km = km_between(lon_a, lat_a, lon_b, lat_b)) # each pair appears twice, as (a, b) and (b, a) error_by_distance <- site_pairs |> filter(km <= 120) |> mutate(band_end = 20 * ceiling(km / 20)) |> summarise(pairs = n() / 2, correlation = cor(error_a, error_b), .by = band_end) |> arrange(band_end) error_by_distance |> mutate(distance = paste0(band_end - 20, "–", band_end, " km"), correlation = round(correlation, 3)) |> select(distance, pairs, correlation) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|distance | pairs| correlation| |:----------|-----:|-----------:| |0–20 km | 285| 0.037| |20–40 km | 925| 0.047| |40–60 km | 1349| -0.014| |60–80 km | 1638| 0.007| |80–100 km | 1788| 0.000| |100–120 km | 1761| -0.018|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} by_site = list(GroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=1) .split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) site_errors = (survey.assign(predicted=out_of_fold(environment, by_site)) .groupby("site_id", as_index=False) .agg(lon=("site_lon", "first"), lat=("site_lat", "first"), caught=("abundance", "sum"), predicted=("predicted", "sum"))) # +1 so that a site with no catch has an error too site_errors["error"] = np.log((site_errors["caught"] + 1) / (site_errors["predicted"] + 1)) site_pairs = site_errors.merge(site_errors, how="cross", suffixes=("_a", "_b")) site_pairs = site_pairs[site_pairs["site_id_a"] != site_pairs["site_id_b"]].copy() site_pairs["km"] = km_between(site_pairs["lon_a"], site_pairs["lat_a"], site_pairs["lon_b"], site_pairs["lat_b"]) # each pair appears twice, as (a, b) and (b, a) nearby = site_pairs[site_pairs["km"] <= 120].copy() nearby["band_end"] = (20 * np.ceil(nearby["km"] / 20)).astype(int) error_by_distance = (nearby.groupby("band_end") .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({"pairs": len(g) // 2, "correlation": g["error_a"].corr(g["error_b"])}), include_groups=False) .reset_index()) error_by_distance.assign( distance=[f"{e - 20}–{e} km" for e in error_by_distance["band_end"]], pairs=error_by_distance["pairs"].astype(int), correlation=error_by_distance["correlation"].round(3), )[["distance", "pairs", "correlation"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | distance | pairs | correlation | |:-----------|--------:|--------------:| | 0–20 km | 285 | 0.067 | | 20–40 km | 925 | 0.071 | | 40–60 km | 1349 | -0.008 | | 60–80 km | 1638 | 0.001 | | 80–100 km | 1788 | -0.008 | | 100–120 km | 1761 | -0.028 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(error_by_distance, aes(band_end - 10, correlation)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_vline(xintercept = patch_km, linetype = "dotted", colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 0.8) + geom_line(colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + geom_point(colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], size = 3) + annotate("text", x = patch_km + 2, y = max(error_by_distance$correlation), label = paste0("range: about ", patch_km, " km"), hjust = 0, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 120, 20), limits = c(0, 120)) + labs(x = "Distance between two sites (km)", y = "Correlation of\ntheir errors", title = paste0("Sites closer than about ", patch_km, " km have errors that lean the same way")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The correlation between the errors of two sites, by the distance between them, for a random forest on the six environmental inputs. Each point is one 20 km band of distances. The correlation is above zero for sites closer than the dotted line and about zero beyond it.](spatial-and-temporal-cv_files/figure-html/fig-correlogram-1.png){#fig-correlogram fig-alt='A line with points, with the distance between two sites in kilometres along the bottom, from 10 to 110, and the correlation of their errors up the side, with a dashed line at zero. The correlation is between 0.037 and 0.047 for sites up to 40 km apart, marked by a dotted vertical line, and stays close to zero, between -0.018 and 0.007, beyond it.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: The correlation is small at every distance, because each site's error rests on a handful of noisy counts. What matters is where it reaches zero. Pairs of sites up to 40 km apart have errors that lean the same way (correlations from 0.037 to 0.047); further apart, they do not. The patches' range is about 40 km. A block of half a degree is 41 km from west to east and 56 km from south to north, at least as wide as the range. That is the size [Spatial and temporal dependence](../06-assumptions-limitations/spatial-and-temporal-dependence.qmd) used. ### The error grows from folds of stations to half-degree blocks The forest on all eight inputs, position included, is cross-validated in three ways: folds of stations, folds of sites, and half-degree blocks. Each run lays the grid of blocks on the map at a random offset, so that the score does not depend on one grid. Every scheme is run 10 times with new folds, because a single run's score depends on how the folds happen to fall. Each run records the pooled RMSE and the median distance to the nearest fitted station. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} score_folds <- function(folds) { predicted <- out_of_fold(all_eight, folds) tibble(rmse = rmse_vec(predicted$abundance, predicted$.pred), nearest_km = median(unlist(map(folds$splits, nearest_km)))) } block_folds <- function(size) { # squares `size` degrees wide, laid at a random offset shift <- runif(2, 0, size) blocked <- mutate(survey, block = paste(floor((site_lon + shift[1]) / size), floor((site_lat + shift[2]) / size))) group_vfold_cv(blocked, group = block, v = 5) } set.seed(2) distance_runs <- map(1:10, \(run) { list("Stations" = vfold_cv(survey, v = 5), "Sites" = group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = 5), "Half-degree blocks" = block_folds(0.5)) |> map(score_folds) |> list_rbind(names_to = "folds") }) |> list_rbind(names_to = "run") distance_runs |> summarise(`nearest fitted station (km)` = mean(nearest_km), `pooled RMSE` = mean(rmse), `spread across runs` = sd(rmse), .by = folds) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|folds | nearest fitted station (km)| pooled RMSE| spread across runs| |:------------------|---------------------------:|-----------:|------------------:| |Stations | 3.98| 4.23| 0.05| |Sites | 8.63| 4.34| 0.09| |Half-degree blocks | 13.04| 4.41| 0.08|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def score_folds(folds): predicted = out_of_fold(all_eight, folds) distance = np.concatenate([nearest_km(fit_rows, held_rows) for fit_rows, held_rows in folds]) return {"rmse": root_mean_squared_error(observed, predicted), "nearest_km": np.median(distance)} rng = np.random.default_rng(2) def block_folds(size, run): # squares size degrees wide, laid at a random offset shift = rng.uniform(0, size, 2) block = (np.floor((survey["site_lon"] + shift[0]) / size).astype(int).astype(str) + " " + np.floor((survey["site_lat"] + shift[1]) / size).astype(int).astype(str)) return list(GroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=run) .split(survey, groups=block)) runs = [] for run in range(10): schemes = { "Stations": list(KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=run) .split(survey)), "Sites": list(GroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=run) .split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])), "Half-degree blocks": block_folds(0.5, run), } runs += [{"run": run, "folds": name, **score_folds(folds)} for name, folds in schemes.items()] distance_runs = pd.DataFrame(runs) (distance_runs.groupby("folds", sort=False) .agg(**{"nearest fitted station (km)": ("nearest_km", "mean"), "pooled RMSE": ("rmse", "mean"), "spread across runs": ("rmse", "std")}) .reset_index() .round(2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | folds | nearest fitted station (km) | pooled RMSE | spread across runs | |:-------------------|------------------------------:|--------------:|---------------------:| | Stations | 3.99 | 4.21 | 0.04 | | Sites | 8.66 | 4.26 | 0.04 | | Half-degree blocks | 13.14 | 4.35 | 0.07 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(distance_runs, aes(nearest_km, rmse)) + geom_point(colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], alpha = 0.3, size = 1.6) + geom_point(data = by_scheme, aes(km, rmse), colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], size = 4) + ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = by_scheme, aes(km, rmse, label = folds), size = 3.4, seed = 4, box.padding = 0.6, min.segment.length = 0.2) + labs(x = "Median distance to the nearest fitted station (km)", y = "Pooled RMSE (individuals)", title = "The error grows as the fitted data lie further away") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The pooled RMSE of the forest on all eight inputs against the median distance from each held-out station to the nearest fitted station. Small points are single runs, large points the average of the 10 runs of each scheme.](spatial-and-temporal-cv_files/figure-html/fig-distance-1.png){#fig-distance fig-alt='A scatter plot of median distance to the nearest fitted station in kilometres, along the bottom, against pooled RMSE in individuals up the side. Three clouds of 10 small points each, with a large point for each average, run from left to right and upwards. Folds of stations sit at 4 km and 4.23; folds of sites at 9 km and 4.34; and half-degree blocks at 13 km and 4.41. Neighbouring clouds overlap up and down.' width=1500} ::: ::: ::: Folds of stations score 4.23, with the nearest fitted station about 4 km away, often at the held-out station's own site. Folds of sites push that to 9 km and the error to 4.34. Half-degree blocks, as wide as the patches, push it to 13 km and the error to 4.41: that is the score to report for a habitat map of new areas. Single runs overlap. The worst run with folds of sites, 4.51, scored higher than the best with blocks, 4.34, so one run of each could have ranked them the other way. Averaged over ten runs, the order follows the distance. ### Forecasting a later year costs little in this survey The survey runs from 2018 to 2023. The expanding window fits the forest to 2018 and 2019 and tests 2020, then adds a year each round up to 2023. For contrast, each of those years is also predicted by a forest fitted to all the other years, later ones included. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} forecast <- map(2020:2023, \(y) { tested <- filter(survey, survey_year == y) predict_from <- function(fitting) { predict(fit(forest_on(all_eight), fitting), tested)$.pred } tibble(year = y, abundance = tested$abundance, earlier = predict_from(filter(survey, survey_year < y)), all_others = predict_from(filter(survey, survey_year != y)), stations_fitted = sum(survey$survey_year < y), site_seen = tested$site_id %in% survey$site_id[survey$survey_year < y]) }) |> list_rbind() forecast |> mutate(year = as.character(year)) |> bind_rows(mutate(forecast, year = "2020–2023", stations_fitted = NA)) |> summarise(`stations fitted, earlier years` = first(stations_fitted), `RMSE, earlier years` = rmse_vec(abundance, earlier), `RMSE, all other years` = rmse_vec(abundance, all_others), .by = year) |> mutate(across(starts_with("RMSE"), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|year | stations fitted, earlier years| RMSE, earlier years| RMSE, all other years| |:---------|------------------------------:|-------------------:|---------------------:| |2020 | 265| 4.64| 4.64| |2021 | 403| 4.11| 4.15| |2022 | 531| 4.02| 3.91| |2023 | 668| 4.77| 4.77| |2020–2023 | | 4.40| 4.38|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} years = survey["survey_year"].to_numpy() sites = survey["site_id"].to_numpy() def predict_from(fit_rows, tested): fitted = forest_on(all_eight).fit(survey.iloc[fit_rows][all_eight], observed[fit_rows]) return fitted.predict(survey.iloc[tested][all_eight]) rounds = [] for y in range(2020, 2024): tested = np.flatnonzero(years == y) rounds.append(pd.DataFrame({ "year": str(y), "abundance": observed[tested], "earlier": predict_from(np.flatnonzero(years < y), tested), "all_others": predict_from(np.flatnonzero(years != y), tested), "stations_fitted": (years < y).sum(), "site_seen": np.isin(sites[tested], sites[years < y])})) forecast = pd.concat(rounds, ignore_index=True) def rmse_pair(g): return {"RMSE, earlier years": root_mean_squared_error(g["abundance"], g["earlier"]), "RMSE, all other years": root_mean_squared_error(g["abundance"], g["all_others"])} table = pd.DataFrame( [{"year": y, "stations fitted, earlier years": g["stations_fitted"].iloc[0], **rmse_pair(g)} for y, g in forecast.groupby("year")] + [{"year": "2020–2023", "stations fitted, earlier years": "", **rmse_pair(forecast)}]) table.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | year | stations fitted, earlier years | RMSE, earlier years | RMSE, all other years | |:----------|---------------------------------:|----------------------:|------------------------:| | 2020 | 265 | 4.75 | 4.69 | | 2021 | 403 | 4.34 | 4.22 | | 2022 | 531 | 3.91 | 3.82 | | 2023 | 668 | 4.73 | 4.73 | | 2020–2023 | | 4.45 | 4.38 | ::: ::: ::: Fitted only to earlier years, the forest scores 4.40 over the four tested years. Fitted to all the other years, it scores 4.38. The gap of 0.02 is small, though the first round was fitted to 265 stations rather than about 670. In this survey a later year looks much like an earlier one, so a model fitted to the past forecasts about as well as one fitted to the other years. That is worth knowing before the model is used next year. Where conditions drift, through warming or a change of gear, the expanding window measures the cost, and leaving one year out hides it, because its models are fitted to the later years that already carry the change. 90% of the tested stations lie at sites visited in an earlier year, so this scores forecasts for the sites already monitored. A forecast for new sites in a later year needs folds of sites inside each round as well. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A cross-validated score says how well a model predicts stations as far from its fitted data as the held-out ones were. Report the **distance to the nearest fitted station** with the score, and choose the folds whose distance matches the use. - A **correlogram** of a model's errors shows how far the patches reach. Here sites up to about 40 km apart had errors that leaned the same way, so half-degree blocks are wide enough. - Averaged over ten runs, the forest's error grew from 4.23 with folds of stations to 4.34 with folds of sites and 4.41 with half-degree blocks. Single runs overlapped, so compare schemes over several runs. - An **expanding window** tests a forecast only on years after those its model was fitted to. Here it scored 4.40, against 4.38 when later years were allowed in. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Draw the correlogram for the forest on all eight inputs, cross-validated by site. Predict first: do its errors still lean the same way at short distances, once the forest knows where each site is? 2. Add blocks a whole degree wide to the ten runs, with `block_folds(1)`. Predict first: does the error keep growing, and do the runs spread more or less than with half-degree blocks, now that the sites fall into fewer blocks? 3. Make the expanding window forecast new sites: in each round, also leave out of the fitted years every visit to the tested year's sites. How much does the forecast's score change?
